newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank slightly tightens money policy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank slightly tightens money policy.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank announced on Thursday a modest tightening of monetary policy by raising two key rates, but pledged to respect market forces as the stock market soars and the local currency slides.
"The reason we raised the rates was to stabilise the foreign exchange market," central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong told reporters after the bank's quarterly meeting.
"All the board members agreed that we should make a small adjustment at this moment," Sheu said of the surprise decision to push rates higher.
"This is a little bit different from our previous monetary policy. You could call it a fine-tuning."
Sheu said the bank board decided to raise the rediscount rate to 5.25 percent from 5.00 percent and accommodations against secured loans to 5.625 percent from 5.375 percent.
Sheu described the central bank's adjusted monetary policy as "not loose, not tight", a slight tightening from his own longtime refrain of "stable to loose, but not too loose".

Sheu insisted that the bank would rely only on macroeconomic money-supply levers to regulate the availability of liquidity in the economy and would leave the Taiwan dollar exchange rate and stock market at the mercy of market forces -- with one caveat.
"The central bank will respect market forces and let market supply and demand determine the Taiwan dollar exchange rates," Sheu said.
"But if there are abnormal factors intervening in the market it will adopt appropriate measures to maintain the foreign exchange market's stability," he said.
Sheu would not say what he meant by "appropriate measures".
"Whether the stock market level is high should be determined by investors and the market," Sheu said.
"When necessary, we will continue to rely on open-market operations to appropriately adjust money-market liquidity," he said.
Sheu said the Taiwan dollar's dramatic recent depreciation did not appear to have resulted from speculative attacks like those that have bedevilled southeast Asia's currencies in July.
"We have not detected obvious speculation," he said.

Sheu said the central bank's repeated recent issuance of billions of Taiwan dollars worth of negotiable certificates of deposit was not intended to cool the stock exchange -- something that many brokers and money dealers have asserted.
"The recent NCD issues have not been aimed at depressing the stock market," he said, repeating what has become a standard central bank explanation.
The stock market has been on an almost unbroken streak since mid-1996, with the index more than doubling in value in that period with the island's electronics sector leading the way.
After a failed bid on Tuesday, the index on Thursday surged comfortably through psychological resistance at 10,000 points to close at 10,066.35, its highest close since early 1990.
